hints: Focus on what electronegativity means, the pull of a nucleus on bonding electrons, and how that pull changes across Period 3.
Remember that nuclear charge increases from Na to Cl while shielding stays similar, so the pull should get steadily stronger with no big dips.
Look for the one smooth, continuously rising graph from Na to Cl, and rule out graphs with peaks or dips at Mg, Al, Si, P or S.
walkthrough:
**Recall the trend in electronegativity**

Think simply. Across Period 3, protons are added but no new shell is added. So effective nuclear charge rises.

Trend rule:
$$\text{electronegativity increases Na < Mg < Al < Si < P < S < Cl}$$

**Predict the shape of the graph**

Because the increase is steady, the graph should rise smoothly from Na to Cl. There should be no sharp peak and no dip down at Al or S.

**Match to the four graphs**

Graph A has a huge peak at Si. Graph B falls all the way. Graph C goes up and down with dips at Al and S. Only one graph shows a steady rise from Na to Cl, and that must be electronegativity.

options.A: Graph A shows a sharp peak at Si with low values at P, S, Cl. This is the melting point trend. Si has a giant covalent structure with very high melting point, while P, S, Cl are simple molecular with low melting points.
options.B: Graph B shows a steady decrease from Na to Cl. This is atomic radius. Increasing nuclear charge pulls the same shells in closer, so atoms get smaller across the period.
options.C: Graph C rises overall but dips at Al and at S. This is first ionisation energy. The dip at Al is due to the 3p electron being easier to remove than 3s, and the dip at S is due to spin-pair repulsion in the 3p orbitals.
options.D: Graph D shows a smooth, continuous increase from Na to Cl. This matches electronegativity perfectly. Greater nuclear charge across the period gives a stronger pull on bonding electrons, so Cl is the most electronegative.
